query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Local compositional segregation at the nanoparticle surface reduces melting onset temperature and initiates partial melting at the surface, progressing inward as temperature increases.
generation.material_initial_state: As-synthesized solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles displaying nominally homogeneous composition at ambient conditions.
generation.intervention: Adjust the temperature ramp rate under in-situ heating (TEM and DSC) from room temperature to above the expected bulk melting range in an inert environment.
generation.conditions: Compare two heating protocols (relatively slow vs. rapid ramps) to observe differences in the onset and progression of melting behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface compositional gradients that induce locally depressed melting temperatures, triggering early localized melting at the surface.
generation.mechanism: Above a critical temperature, preferential diffusion of selected elements to the surface lowers the local melting point, causing a surface-first transition that then propagates inward.
generation.predicted_outcome: Faster heating will show earlier localized melting and partial lattice disorder at the particle surface in both TEM imaging and DSC measurements, while slower heating will delay but not eliminate the same surface-initiated melting pathway.
generation.baseline: Under a single slow heating rate, the melting onset is slightly higher and more gradual, with fewer compositional gradients in the as-heated nanoparticles.
generation.boundary: This effect depends on partial immiscibility that drives surface segregation; under conditions with fully ideal mixing or non-inert atmospheres, the phenomenon may be less pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: Exact degrees of surface segregation and the precise temperature thresholds for premelting cannot be fully quantified from current data alone.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in-situ heating experiments with detailed composition mapping via EDS and electron diffraction at multiple heating rates to detect where and when melting initiates in each nanoparticle.
measurements: Surface vs. core chemical compositions with increasing temperature
Electron diffraction or imaging to detect onset of partial melting
DSC to measure changes in heat flow at hypothesized melting transitions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no preferential surface-initiated melting or associated compositional gradients are observed under either slow or rapid heating, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Bulk materials have very low dispersion, i.e., a low ratio of surface to bulk atoms. A large surface-to-bulk atom ratio is, however, vital for efficient catalysts. Nanoparticles possess such high dispersion. This generates a large interest in developing HEA nanoparticle synthesis methods. Many synthesis methods for HEA nanoparticles are high-energy shock methods such as Joule-heating, microwave heating, laser-ablation, and fast-bed pyrolysis. Recent studies propose that it is also possible to use low-temperature solution-based techniques to synthesize HEA nanoparticles or low-temperature reduction of solid precursors. Such methods open for fine-tuning both the composition and nanostructure of nanoparticles. For high-temperature synthesis approaches, entropy plays a role in stabilizing the multi-metallic phases, so that single-phase materials can be prepared. Thermal shock methods are also believed to freeze the material in a state of high entropy during controlled cool-down. The structural stability of the prototype CoCrFeMnNi HEA has been extensively studied in a wide temperature range from 55 K to its melting temperature of ∼1,600 K at ambient pressure but to our knowledge, no polymorphic transition has been observed. Conversely, high-pressure studies remain a virgin area in HEAs. In this work, using in situ high-pressure XRD techniques, we observed the first polymorphic transition from fcc to hcp in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA, as shown in Fig. 1c. Therefore, some critical questions are how and why can an hcp HEA form at high-pressure and can it be maintained at ambient conditions? According to the d-spacing of the main reflections of both fcc and hcp (that is, (111) and (220) of fcc, and (100), (002), (101) and (110) of hcp, as a function of pressure shown in Fig. 2a), it is clear that the hcp-(002) and hcp-(110) planes inherit the fcc-(111) and fcc-(220) planes, respectively. In addition, Fig. 2b shows no obvious volume collapse during the transition; both the fcc and hcp phases seem to have almost the same volume per atom and bulk modulus. AbstractDirect formation of ultra-small nanoparticles on carbon supports by rapid high temperature synthesis method offers new opportunities for scalable nanomanufacturing and the synthesis of stable multi-elemental nanoparticles. However, the underlying mechanisms affecting the dispersion and stability of nanoparticles on the supports during high temperature processing remain enigmatic. In this work, we report the observation of metallic nanoparticles formation and stabilization on carbon supports through in situ Joule heating method. We find that the formation of metallic nanoparticles is associated with the simultaneous phase transition of amorphous carbon to a highly defective turbostratic graphite (T-graphite). Molecular dynamic (MD) simulations suggest that the defective T-graphite provide numerous nucleation sites for the nanoparticles to form. Furthermore, the nanoparticles partially intercalate and take root on edge planes, leading to high binding energy on support. This interaction between nanoparticles and T-graphite substrate strengthens the anchoring and provides excellent thermal stability to the nanoparticles. chosen.why: We propose a mechanistic hypothesis that localized compositional segregation, particularly at the nanoparticle surface, reduces the local melting temperature and initiates phase transition and partial melting from the surface inward. A controlled comparison measuring in-situ structure and phase transitions under varying temperature ramp rates allows correlation of morphological and compositional changes with the onset and progression of melting. Prior studies on multicomponent nanoparticles have shown that surface effects can significantly alter phase transition temperatures. Observing an absence of surface-initiated melting onset or a lack of compositional gradients would falsify this hypothesis.
